name: Bl. Beatrice I and Bl. Beatrice II d'Este
title: Benedictine nuns of the house of Este
summary: Bl. Beatrice I and Bl. Beatrice II d'Este, an aunt and her niece of the noble house of Este, left the court to become Benedictine nuns. Each founded a convent, Beatrice I on Monte Gemola and Beatrice II in Ferrara after her betrothed died in battle. They have no widely recognized patronage, but they kept the same Rule the monks of St. Bernard keep today.
life: The Este were one of the great noble families of northern Italy. They took their name from the town of Este, below the Euganean Hills near Padua, and later ruled Ferrara and then Modena. Two daughters of this house, an aunt and her niece, both named Beatrice, left the life of the court to become Benedictine nuns. Both are honored as Blessed. What we know of them comes from short medieval lives and from the long memory of the convents they founded, so the outline is firmer than the details.

Beatrice I was a daughter of Azzo VI, lord of Este. She grew up at the family's castle and, as a young woman, refused the marriage her family could have arranged. She took the veil among Benedictine nuns and then founded a small community of her own on Monte Gemola, a quiet hill in the Euganean range. There she lived a plain life of prayer and work with a few companions, and there she died young, in 1226, probably in her early thirties. Her cult was confirmed by Pope Clement XIII in 1763.

Beatrice II was the daughter of Beatrice I's brother, Azzo VII. Her family promised her in marriage to a nobleman, Galeazzo Manfredi. He died of wounds received in battle before the wedding could take place. Beatrice did not look for another match. She entered religious life and, with her father's help, founded the convent of Sant'Antonio in Polesine in Ferrara, where she lived under the Rule of St. Benedict until her death on 18 January 1262. Benedictine nuns still live there. Her cult was confirmed by Pope Clement XIV in 1774.

Neither woman did anything the world would call great. They prayed, they worked, they kept the Rule, and they each left behind a house where others could do the same. The labels in the abbey's reliquary, "B. Beat. I. Est." and "B. Beat. II. Est.", still give them the title Blessed, which is the title they hold today.
why_here: These two are the only Benedictine nuns in the abbey's reliquary, and they lived the same Rule the monks of St. Bernard keep today. Both chose a hidden life of stability over the position their family could give them. Beatrice II made that choice after a loss that might have broken her, and she built something lasting out of it.

For the Prep's young women, many of them living away from home, these two show that a strong and free choice about one's life can be made young. For the monks, they are a reminder that a monastery is founded and kept alive by ordinary faithful days more than by famous deeds. Their prayers suit anyone who has had a plan collapse and must decide what to build next.
relic: Two relics on the oval of royal saints and saints of the House of Este (IMG_4912–4915), labelled "B. Beat. I. Est." and "B. Beat. II. Est."
check: Neither has a widely recognized patronage, so the list is left empty. Some sources give Beatrice II's feast as 19 January (allowed by Pius VI) rather than 18 January, her death day; please check which date the abbey prefers. Beatrice II's death is given as 1262 by most sources, 1264 by a few.

name: St. Benedict of Nursia
title: Abbot, father of Western monks
feast: 11 July (21 March in the monastic calendar)
summary: St. Benedict of Nursia, known to us mainly through the Dialogues of St. Gregory the Great, lived as a hermit at Subiaco and founded Monte Cassino, where he wrote the Rule that most Western monasteries came to follow. He is patron of Europe and of a good death. Every day at St. Bernard Abbey, from the Office to the bakery, is shaped by his Rule.
life: Almost everything we know of Benedict's life comes from one book, the second book of the Dialogues of Pope St. Gregory the Great, written about fifty years after Benedict's death. Gregory names the monks who told him the stories, but he wrote to build up faith, not as a modern historian, and his account is full of wonders. The life below follows Gregory. The plain outline is likely enough. The miracles are best read as the way his first disciples remembered him.

Benedict was born at Nursia (Norcia) in the hills of Umbria, of a free and well-to-do family. Tradition holds that St. Scholastica was his twin sister. He was sent to Rome to study, but the loose life of the city drove him out. He went to Subiaco, east of Rome, and lived for about three years as a hermit in a cave, fed by a monk named Romanus who let down bread on a rope. His name spread, and a community of monks at Vicovaro asked him to be their abbot. His strictness soon wearied them, and Gregory says they put poison in his wine. When Benedict made the sign of the cross over the cup, it shattered. He left them, and at Subiaco he founded twelve small monasteries for the many who came to him.

About 529 he moved south to Monte Cassino, a height above the road from Rome to Naples, where he pulled down an old pagan shrine and built a monastery. There he wrote his Rule. He calls it "a little rule for beginners". Its seventy-three short chapters lay out a whole life. The monks pray the Divine Office together at set hours, which Benedict calls the Work of God. They work with their hands, read Scripture slowly, and live under an abbot who stands in the place of Christ but must answer to God for every soul. The monk promises stability, obedience and conversatio morum, a lifelong turning of his ways toward God. The Rule is strict, but it makes room for the young, the old, the sick and the weak, and it asks the abbot to temper everything so that the strong have something to strive for and the weak are not driven away. The phrase ora et labora, "pray and work", is a later summary of the Rule, not words from it.

Gregory says that Benedict met his sister Scholastica once a year near Monte Cassino, and that on their last visit a storm she had prayed for kept him with her through the night, talking of heaven. She died three days later. In 547, or soon after, Benedict had his grave opened. Six days later, Gregory writes, he had himself carried into the chapel, received the Body and Blood of the Lord, and died standing, his arms raised in prayer and held up by his monks. That death is the reason he is invoked for a good death.

The Rule outlived its author. Monte Cassino was destroyed by the Lombards, by Saracens, and in 1944 by Allied bombing, and was rebuilt each time. Both Monte Cassino and the French abbey of Fleury (Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire) claim his bones. By the 9th century his Rule had become the rule of most monasteries in the West, and the monks who lived it kept learning, farming and the liturgy alive across Europe for centuries. For that reason Pope St. Paul VI named him patron of Europe in 1964.
patronage: monks, nuns and all who live under his Rule
against temptation and evil (especially through the St. Benedict medal)
why_here: Every day at St. Bernard Abbey is shaped by Benedict's Rule. It sets the hours of Matins, Vespers and Compline, the work in the bakery, the farm and the Grotto, the care of the guests and of the old monks in the infirmary, and the vows each monk makes. Benedict is the father of this house in the plainest sense. When the monks ask his prayers they ask for faithfulness to the life he wrote down. Br. Benedict, the head baker and oblate director, bears his name, and the oblates who share the life from outside the cloister follow his Rule too.

For the Prep, Benedict is a patron of schoolchildren in some places, and his Rule is about learning to live with others, to listen (its first word is "Listen"), and to keep at a good thing for a long time. Boarders far from home live a little like his monks. He is also the one to ask for a good death, for the monks in the infirmary and those buried in the abbey cemetery.
relic: Two relics: a cross-shaped gold reliquary labelled "[S.] Benedicti Abb." (IMG_4916), and a theca on the large linen board labelled "S. Benedicti Ab. C." (of St. Benedict, Abbot and Confessor).
check: Patronage of schoolchildren and of farmers is traditional and local, not official; keep or drop as you prefer.

name: St. Bernadette Soubirous
title: Visionary of Lourdes, Sister of Charity of Nevers
summary: St. Bernadette Soubirous was a poor, sickly girl of Lourdes who said that in 1858 a lady appeared to her eighteen times at the grotto of Massabielle, a private revelation the Church has approved. She later became a Sister of Charity at Nevers and is a patron of the sick and the poor. She is a natural friend to the monks who keep the Ave Maria Grotto.
life: Bernadette Soubirous was born in Lourdes, in the foothills of the Pyrenees, on 7 January 1844, the eldest child of a miller. The family lost its mill and fell into poverty, and by 1857 they were living in a damp former jail cell called the cachot. Bernadette suffered from asthma, had little schooling and spoke the local dialect rather than French. At fourteen she had not yet made her First Communion because she could not learn the catechism.

On 11 February 1858, while gathering firewood by the river Gave, she saw at the mouth of a grotto called Massabielle a young lady dressed in white with a blue sash. Over the next months she said the lady appeared to her eighteen times. The lady asked for prayer and penance for sinners and for a chapel to be built, and told Bernadette to drink from a spring. Bernadette dug in the mud of the grotto, and a spring began to flow there. On 25 March the lady said, "I am the Immaculate Conception", words Bernadette did not understand but repeated to the parish priest. The town was divided. Bernadette was questioned by the police and the clergy many times. She never changed her account and never took money or gifts.

In 1862 the bishop of Tarbes declared that the faithful could believe the apparitions were real. The Church's approval of Lourdes, like that of Fatima, is approval of a private revelation, which no one is bound to believe. Pilgrims began to come in great numbers, and many cures have been claimed at the spring. The Church has recognized only a few of them as miraculous, after long medical study.

Bernadette wanted to get away from the crowds. In 1866 she joined the Sisters of Charity of Nevers and took the name Marie-Bernard. She never saw Lourdes again. She worked as an assistant in the infirmary and then in the sacristy, and she was often ill herself. When a superior treated her coldly, she bore it without complaint. She said that her task was to be ill, and that the Blessed Virgin had used her like a broom and then put her back in her corner. She died at Nevers on 16 April 1879, aged 35, of tuberculosis of the bone. She was canonized by Pius XI in 1933. Her body, found well preserved when it was exhumed, lies in a glass shrine at Nevers.
why_here: Lourdes is a grotto, and the abbey's best-known work is a grotto too. Br. Joseph Zoettl built the Ave Maria Grotto out of stone, shells, glass and scrap, a poor man's work in praise of Our Lady, and it has drawn pilgrims to Cullman since 1934. Bernadette, a poor girl at a cave by a river, is a natural friend to that work and to the monks who keep it.

She also fits the Prep. She was behind in school, unsure of herself, and questioned by people who thought her foolish, yet she told the truth plainly and would not be bought. For a student who feels slow or out of place, or who is laughed at for believing, she is a good companion. Her years in the infirmary make her a friend of the abbey's sick monks too.
relic: One relic on the large linen board, labelled "S. M. Bernardae" (of St. Maria Bernarda, her name as a sister).
check: The catalogue does not say whether the Ave Maria Grotto includes a Lourdes miniature; if it does, the link is worth naming.

name: St. Bernard of Clairvaux
title: Abbot and Doctor of the Church, patron of this abbey
summary: St. Bernard of Clairvaux brought some thirty relatives and friends into the poor monastery of Cîteaux, was abbot of Clairvaux for thirty-eight years, and spread the Cistercians across Europe. A Doctor of the Church, he is best known for his writing on the love of God and on Our Lady, and he is a patron of beekeepers. He is the patron of this abbey and its school.
life: Bernard was born in 1090 at Fontaines, near Dijon in Burgundy, one of seven children of a knight. His mother, Aleth, was devout and he was close to her, and her death when he was a young man moved him deeply. He was clever, well read and good company, and could have had a career in the world or in the Church. Instead, about 1112 or 1113, he knocked at the gate of Cîteaux, a new and very poor monastery that wanted to keep the Rule of St. Benedict to the letter. He did not come alone. He brought some thirty relatives and friends with him, among them several of his brothers, whom he had talked into the life one by one.

Cîteaux had been close to dying out. After Bernard's arrival it grew so fast that within three years it was sending out monks to found new houses. In 1115 Bernard, then about twenty-five, was sent with twelve monks to a wild valley in Champagne. They called it Clairvaux, the clear valley. The first years were hard, with poor food and fierce fasting, and Bernard later admitted he had been too severe with himself and with others. He was abbot of Clairvaux for thirty-eight years. From it some sixty-eight new monasteries were founded in his lifetime, and through him the Cistercians, the reformed Benedictines of Cîteaux, spread across Europe.

Bernard never wanted to leave his cloister, but popes, kings and bishops kept calling him out of it. When two men were elected pope in 1130, he travelled for years to win the Church over to Innocent II, and the schism ended in 1138. One of his own monks became Pope Eugene III, and Bernard wrote him a book, On Consideration, warning him not to let business crowd out prayer. He opposed the teaching of Peter Abelard and had it condemned at Sens in 1141. In 1146, at the pope's request, he preached the Second Crusade at Vézelay. The crusade ended in disaster, and Bernard took the blame bitterly. When a monk preached that the crusaders should first kill the Jews of the Rhineland, Bernard went to Germany himself, stopped him and defended the Jews. Some of his actions, and his harshness in argument, are hard to admire today. He was a great man, and also a difficult one.

He was above all a writer and preacher on the love of God. In On Loving God he says that the reason for loving God is God himself, and the measure is to love without measure. His eighty-six sermons on the Song of Songs, given to his monks over eighteen years, read the love poem as the story of God and the soul. He wrote and preached on Our Lady with warmth, and his homily on the Annunciation gave the Church the words "Look to the star, call upon Mary." The famous prayer called the Memorare is often credited to him, but in its present form it comes from a later time. Dante, in the last cantos of the Paradiso, chose Bernard to lead him to the vision of God and put in his mouth the great prayer to the Virgin.

Bernard died at Clairvaux on 20 August 1153. He was canonized in 1174, only twenty-one years later, and Pope Pius VIII declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1830. He is called the "Mellifluous Doctor", the teacher whose words flow like honey, and in 1953 Pope Pius XII wrote an encyclical on him with that title, Doctor Mellifluus. He is often shown with a beehive, and for that reason he became the patron of beekeepers and of candle makers, who work with wax. Images of him often show the white Cistercian habit, a book, and Our Lady.
patronage: St. Bernard Abbey and St. Bernard Preparatory School
why_here: Bernard is the patron of this abbey and its school, and his name is on everything here, from the Prep to the Clairvaux Society that supports both. He was a Benedictine by Rule, one who wanted to live it more simply and fully, and he trained a great many young men to do the same. That makes him a fitting patron for a community whose vocations are increasing. His life also shows the strain between the cloister and the work outside it, a strain the monks know when they teach, coach, run a Retreat Center and keep the Grotto.

For the Prep, he is the young man who chose his path at twenty-two and brought his friends with him, and a writer whose Latin is still read. His honey and wax link him to the monks' candle making. He also knew failure, after the Second Crusade, and kept going. The abbey keeps four relics of him, as many as of any saint in the reliquary.
relic: Four relics: a round gold reliquary ringed with rhinestones, "S. Bernardi Ab. D." (IMG_4885); a gilt Gothic tabernacle, "S. Bernardi" (4976); a gilt theca with open loops, "S. Bern. A. D." (4991); and one label on the oval of fifteen relics (4965).
check: The abbey's own reason for taking St. Bernard as patron in 1891 is not in the sources given; if it is known, it would be worth a sentence. The count of about sixty-eight foundations from Clairvaux in his lifetime is the usual figure; please check against your preferred source.

name: St. Blaise
title: Bishop and martyr
summary: St. Blaise is said to have been bishop of Sebaste in Armenia and a martyr about 316, but little beyond his name, his town and his death is certain. A legend that he healed a boy choking on a fish bone made him the patron against ailments of the throat and of wool combers. Each 3 February the monks give the Prep his blessing of throats.
life: St. Blaise is one of the most loved saints of the Middle Ages and one of the least known to history. He is said to have been bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, now Sivas in Turkey, and to have been martyred about 316 under the Emperor Licinius, who persecuted Christians in the East after Constantine had made peace with the Church in the West. Almost nothing beyond his name, his town and his death is certain. His written Acts are late and full of legend.

The earliest firm trace of his cult is medical. Aëtius of Amida, a Greek physician of the 6th century, told doctors treating a patient with something stuck in the throat to call on "Blaise, martyr and servant of Christ". The legend explains why. As Blaise was being led to prison, a mother brought him her son, who was choking to death on a fish bone. Blaise prayed over the boy and he was healed.

Other stories filled out his life. He is said to have fled persecution and lived in a cave, where wild animals came to him to be healed. A poor woman's pig was carried off by a wolf, and at Blaise's word the wolf brought it back. When he was in prison, the woman brought him food and candles. The legend says his flesh was torn with iron combs, the kind used to card wool, before he was beheaded. From that story he became the patron of wool combers.

His cult spread widely in the East and the West. He was counted among the Fourteen Holy Helpers, saints invoked together in the Rhineland and Bavaria for help in particular troubles. Dubrovnik on the Adriatic took him as its patron. On his feast, priests still bless throats with two crossed candles, praying that through his intercession the person may be kept from ailments of the throat and from every other illness.
why_here: The blessing of throats on 3 February is one of the few rites of the year that reaches every student in a Catholic school, and at the Prep it is the monks who give it. A choir monk sings the Office several times a day, and teachers, choirmasters and coaches use their voices all day long. Blaise is a practical patron for all of them.

He was also one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, a devotion of the German and Bavarian Catholics from whom the abbey and Cullman both descend. His legends are honest about what they are, stories of care for a frightened mother, a choking child, a poor woman's pig, and the animals of the wild. A monastery with a cattle farm and chickens can take that last one in good humor.
relic: One relic on the large linen board, labelled for St. Blaise.

name: St. Bonaventure
title: Franciscan, cardinal, the Seraphic Doctor
summary: St. Bonaventure was a Franciscan friar, a master of theology at Paris alongside St. Thomas Aquinas, and for seventeen years the minister general who held a divided order together. A Doctor of the Church called the Seraphic Doctor, he is a patron of theologians and of his hometown, Bagnoregio. He is a scholar's saint for the Prep and a model of patient governance for the abbey.
life: Bonaventure was born Giovanni di Fidanza at Bagnoregio, a hill town near Viterbo, about 1217 (some say 1221). His father was a physician. Later he wrote that as a small boy he had been cured of a grave illness through the prayers of St. Francis, and the story that Francis himself greeted him with "O buona ventura", "Oh, good fortune", is a legend. He went to Paris to study and there joined the Franciscan friars, about 1243. He studied under Alexander of Hales and became a master of theology. He and St. Thomas Aquinas were received as masters at the university at the same time, in 1257, after a long quarrel over whether the begging friars should teach there at all.

In 1257 he was elected minister general of the Franciscans. The order was large and divided. Some friars wanted to keep Francis's poverty to the letter, others had settled into houses and schools, and a radical party was spreading wild prophecies about the end of the age. Bonaventure led them for seventeen years. He wrote constitutions for the order, visited its houses on foot, and steered a middle path that kept both poverty and learning. In 1263 he finished the Major Life of St. Francis, which the order made its official life, and soon after the earlier lives were ordered destroyed. Historians still argue about that decision.

He was a theologian of the heart as well as the head. In 1259, on Mount La Verna, where Francis had received the stigmata, he wrote The Journey of the Mind into God, a short book that leads the reader from the things of the world, through the soul, to God, and ends in love rather than knowledge. His Breviloquium is a compact summary of the faith. He taught that all learning should lead to holiness.

Pope Gregory X made him cardinal-bishop of Albano in 1273. A story says that the messengers who brought the cardinal's hat found him washing dishes and asked them to hang it on a tree until he had finished. He helped prepare the Second Council of Lyon, which tried to reunite the Greek and Latin churches, and died during it on 15 July 1274. He was canonized in 1482 and named a Doctor of the Church in 1588, with the title "Seraphic Doctor".
why_here: Bonaventure held a divided community together for seventeen years without forcing it into one shape, by patience, visits and clear rules. Any abbot and his council could ask his prayers for that kind of steady governance. He also never set study against prayer, which is the Benedictine instinct too.

For the Prep he is a scholar's saint. He was a colleague, and sometimes a rival, of St. Thomas Aquinas, the patron of Br. Thomas, the abbey's librarian, and the two of them stand together as the great teachers of the 13th century. Theology and Latin teachers at the Prep teach in the tradition he helped build. The dish-washing story, legend though it is, is a fair lesson for students who are good at their books.
relic: One relic on the large oval of fifteen relics in a pewter-coloured frame (IMG_4965), labelled for St. Bonaventure.
check: His birth year is given as 1217 or 1221. The patronage of theologians is customary but not formally declared.

name: St. Camillus de Lellis
title: Founder of the Ministers of the Sick
feast: 14 July (18 July in the United States)
summary: St. Camillus de Lellis was a soldier and gambler who, after his conversion, founded the Ministers of the Sick, men who vowed to nurse the sick even at the risk of their own lives. Leo XIII named him patron of the sick and of hospitals, and Pius XI added nurses. The abbey honors monks who nursed the sick in epidemics, and he suits its infirmary.
life: Camillus was born in 1550 at Bucchianico in the Abruzzi, in southern Italy. His mother was nearly sixty and died when he was a boy. His father was a soldier, often away, and Camillus grew up with little guidance. He was very tall, with a quick temper and a passion for cards and dice. As a young man he went soldiering as a mercenary, fought for Venice against the Turks, and gambled away all he had. In 1574 he was in Naples with nothing left, he is said to have lost even his shirt, and he took work as a laborer on a building for the Capuchin friars at Manfredonia.

There, in February 1575, after a talk with one of the friars, he was converted. He tried twice to become a Capuchin, but each time a sore on his leg that would not heal forced him to leave. The wound took him to the hospital of San Giacomo in Rome, first as a patient and then as a servant, and in time he became its master of the house. He was shocked by what he saw. The sick were left dirty, unfed and alone, and hired attendants were often cruel. He gathered a few men who would nurse the sick for the love of God, as a mother nurses her only child.

With St. Philip Neri as his confessor, he studied for the priesthood in his thirties, alongside boys, and was ordained in 1584. His company, the Ministers of the Sick, was approved in 1586. The members wore a large red cross on their habits and added a fourth vow to serve the sick even at the risk of their own lives. They nursed in the hospitals of Rome and Naples, on the ships of the plague-stricken, and on the battlefields of Hungary and Croatia, and many of them died of the diseases they nursed.

Camillus himself was ill for much of his life, with the leg wound, a rupture and other pains, yet he would still go from bed to bed in the night. He resigned as superior general in 1607 and died in Rome on 14 July 1614. He was canonized in 1746. Pope Leo XIII named him, with St. John of God, patron of the sick and of hospitals in 1886, and Pius XI added nurses in 1930.
why_here: The abbey honors monks who did exactly what Camillus asked of his men. Abbot Benedict Menges nursed the sick in the yellow fever of 1878. Frater Hubert Carney died in 1918 nursing others in the influenza. Fr. Urban Tracy served lepers. Camillus would have recognized them. His prayers are fitting for the brothers who now care for the old and sick monks in the abbey infirmary, and for the monks who are patients there.

He is also a saint for young people who start badly. He was a gambler and a brawler in his twenties and found his life's work only after he had wrecked his plans. A Prep student who has made a mess of things, or who is thinking about nursing or medicine, could do worse than ask his help.
relic: Two relics: a sunburst stand and pendant (IMG_4872, 4875, 4876, 4883), and a theca on the large linen board labelled for St. Camillus de Lellis.
check: The papal patronages (Leo XIII 1886 for the sick and hospitals, Pius XI 1930 for nurses) are as usually given; worth confirming.

name: St. Catherine Labouré
title: Daughter of Charity, visionary of the Miraculous Medal
summary: St. Catherine Labouré was a farmer's daughter who became a Daughter of Charity and said that in 1830 Our Lady asked her to have the Miraculous Medal made. She kept that secret for decades while caring for old men, minding a door and keeping poultry. A patron of the elderly by tradition, she shows the monks that such humble work can be the whole of a holy life.
life: Zoé Labouré was born in 1806 at Fain-lès-Moutiers in Burgundy, one of the many children of a farmer. Her mother died when she was nine, and the story is told that she took a statue of Our Lady in her arms and asked her to be her mother now. From about twelve she ran her father's house and farm, with its kitchen, its laborers and its dovecote. She did not learn to read and write until much later. Her father opposed her wish to be a nun, but at twenty-four she was received into the Daughters of Charity of St. Vincent de Paul and took the name Catherine.

In 1830, as a novice in the convent in the Rue du Bac in Paris, she said she was woken one July night by a child who led her to the chapel, where Our Lady sat and spoke with her for hours. On 27 November she said she saw Mary standing on a globe with rays of light from her hands, framed by the words "O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to you", and then the reverse, an M with a cross and two hearts. She was told to have a medal made. Her confessor, Fr. Aladel, was slow to believe her, but in 1832, with the archbishop's leave, the first medals were struck. Paris was suffering an outbreak of cholera, and the medal spread so fast and with so many reported cures that people began calling it the Miraculous Medal.
These apparitions are a private revelation, which no one is bound to believe. The medal itself is a sacramental, a sign that leads to prayer, not a charm.

Catherine asked that her name be kept secret, and it was. For about forty-five years she worked at a hospice for old men at Reuilly, outside Paris. She minded the door, did the laundry, cooked, and kept the poultry, and the other sisters thought her plain and rather dull. Only months before her death on 31 December 1876 did she tell her superior that she was the sister of the medal. She was canonized by Pius XII in 1947. Her body rests in the chapel of the Rue du Bac.
patronage: those who wear the Miraculous Medal
why_here: Catherine spent most of her life caring for old men, answering a door and keeping chickens, and no one knew who she was. A monastery with an infirmary for its old and sick monks, guest masters at the door, and some forty chickens on its farm has plenty of that kind of work. She shows that it can be the whole of a holy life.

She also grew up running a farmhouse at twelve after her mother's death and could not read until she was grown. For a Prep student who carries more at home than classmates know, or who came late to learning, she is a quiet ally. Many families at the school will have a Miraculous Medal in a drawer, and her story gives them its history.
relic: Two relics: one in a gilt pendant on the large linen board shared with St. Philip Neri and St. John Vianney, and one in a gilt crown-of-thorns pendant in the white linen case (IMG_4981).
check: Her patronage of the elderly is popular rather than official.

name: St. Catherine of Siena
title: Dominican tertiary, Doctor of the Church
summary: St. Catherine of Siena, a wool dyer's daughter with little schooling, nursed the sick through the plague and dictated hundreds of letters, urging Pope Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome. A Doctor of the Church, she is patron of Italy and co-patron of Europe. She shows the Prep's students that a young person can speak to those in charge with courage and charity.
life: Caterina Benincasa was born in Siena in 1347, the twenty-fourth child of a wool dyer, Jacopo, and his wife Lapa. Her twin sister died as a baby. From childhood she was drawn to prayer. When her family began to arrange a marriage for her in her teens, she cut off her hair, and they punished her by making her the household servant. She did the work without complaint, and her father in the end let her be. At about sixteen she was received among the Mantellate, Dominican lay women who wore the habit but lived in their own homes.

For three years she lived almost in silence in a small room in her father's house. Then she came out to serve. She nursed the sick in Siena's hospitals, including those whose diseases others shunned, and stayed with the dying during the plague of 1374. She visited prisoners, and is said to have walked with a young man condemned to death to the scaffold, holding his head as he died. A circle of friends, priests, nobles and poor women, gathered round her and called her "Mamma".

She learned to read as a young woman and to write only late in her short life, but she dictated hundreds of letters to popes, kings, captains and ordinary people. About 380 survive. In them she wrote bluntly to Pope Gregory XI, then living at Avignon in France, and urged him to come back to Rome and to reform the Church. She went to Avignon in 1376 to tell him in person. He returned to Rome in 1377. When the Great Schism broke out the next year, she threw her strength behind Pope Urban VI. Her book, The Dialogue, is a conversation between the soul and God about truth, love and the Church.

Worn out by fasting and labor, she died in Rome on 29 April 1380, aged thirty-three. She was canonized in 1461. Pius XII named her, with St. Francis, patron of Italy in 1939. In 1970 Paul VI made her one of the first two women Doctors of the Church, with St. Teresa of Ávila, and in 1999 John Paul II named her a co-patron of Europe.
why_here: Catherine had no title, no office and little schooling, and she still told a pope to his face what he needed to hear. She shows the Prep's students, girls especially, that a young person can speak with courage and charity to those in charge, and that conviction is worth more when it is joined to service. She did her first great work in her teens and early twenties.

For the monks she is a reminder that prayer and action are not rivals. She lived three years in near silence and then nursed plague victims and wrote to princes. She also loved the Church enough to criticize it honestly and stay in it, which is a grace every religious community needs.
relic: One relic on the large oval of fifteen relics in a pewter-coloured frame (IMG_4965), labelled for St. Catherine of Siena.

name: St. Charbel Makhlouf
title: Maronite monk and hermit
summary: St. Charbel Makhlouf was a Lebanese Maronite monk who spent sixteen years in the monastery of Annaya and twenty-three as a hermit above it, praying, working the land and keeping silence. Many healings have been reported since his death, and he is a patron of Lebanon and of the sick. He is a brother across rites to monks who vow stability and work the abbey's land.
life: Youssef Makhlouf was born in 1828 at Bekaa Kafra, a high mountain village in northern Lebanon. His father, a mule driver, died when he was three, and an uncle raised him. As a boy he tended the family's cow and was known for praying in a cave near the village. Two of his mother's brothers were hermits, and he visited them often. At twenty-three he left home without telling his family and entered the Lebanese Maronite Order, at the monastery of Our Lady of Mayfouk. He took the name Charbel, after an early martyr of Edessa.

The Maronites are Eastern Catholics, in full communion with Rome, whose liturgy is in Syriac and Arabic. Charbel studied theology at the monastery of Kfifan, where one of his teachers was St. Nimatullah Kassab Al-Hardini, also a monk and now also a saint. He was ordained priest in 1859 and sent to the monastery of St. Maron at Annaya. For sixteen years he lived there as an ordinary monk, praying the Office, working in the fields and vineyards, and keeping silence and obedience so exactly that others noticed.

In 1875 he was allowed to move to the hermitage of Sts. Peter and Paul, on the hill above Annaya. He lived there for twenty-three years under a strict rule, eating once a day, sleeping little on a mat of leaves, working the hermitage land and spending long hours before the Blessed Sacrament. In December 1898 he suffered a stroke while saying Mass, and he died on Christmas Eve.

After his burial, people reported a bright light over his grave. When the tomb was opened some months later, the body was found to be intact and seeping a fluid like sweat and blood, and many reports of healing followed. These reports, and the state of the body, drew pilgrims from all over Lebanon and beyond. The Church did not rest his cause on the body, but on his life and on cures it examined. Paul VI beatified him at the close of the Second Vatican Council in 1965 and canonized him in 1977.
why_here: Charbel was a monk who spent his whole life within a few miles of one monastery, praying the Office, working the land and keeping silence. Nothing he did would make the news, and that is the point. The monks of St. Bernard make a vow of stability, and many of them work the abbey's farm, garden and grounds. Charbel is a brother to them across the Mediterranean and across rites.

He is also a reminder that the Benedictine West is not the whole of monastic life. The Eastern monks, of whom he is the best known in modern times, keep traditions older than Benedict. Students who come to the Prep from abroad, or from Eastern Catholic families, may find in him a saint of their own.
relic: One relic on the large linen board, labelled "S." (Saint) Charbel, so written after his canonization in 1977.
check: Some sources give his time in the hermitage as twenty-three years (1875–1898), the catalogue's figure. His patronage of monks and hermits is natural rather than formally declared.

name: St. Clare of Assisi
title: Founder of the Poor Clares
summary: St. Clare of Assisi left her noble family at eighteen to follow St. Francis, who cut off her hair, and she lived over forty years in poverty and prayer at San Damiano. She wrote the first rule for women written by a woman, and Pius XII named her patron of television. The abbey's relic of her is a lock of that hair, the sign of a young person's choice.
life: Chiara Offreduccio was born in Assisi in 1194, into a noble family. As a girl she was known for her prayer and her gifts to the poor. When she was about eighteen she heard Francis of Assisi preach, and met him in secret several times. On the night after Palm Sunday 1212, she slipped out of her family's house by a side door and went to the little chapel of the Porziuncola, where Francis and his brothers met her with torches. Francis cut off her hair as a sign that she now belonged to God, and she put on a rough habit. Her family came to drag her home, but she held to the altar and showed them her shorn head, and they gave up. Within weeks her younger sister Agnes joined her.

After short stays with Benedictine nuns, Clare and her sisters settled at San Damiano, the small church outside Assisi that Francis had rebuilt with his own hands. She lived there for forty-one years and hardly left. The sisters prayed, worked with their hands, and owned nothing. Clare spun thread and sewed altar linens for poor churches even when she was confined to bed. She fought for years for the right of her community to have no property or income at all, and got it as a "privilege of poverty" from the pope. She cared for Francis in his last illness and outlived him by twenty-seven years.

Tradition tells that in 1240, when soldiers of the Emperor Frederick II, many of them Saracens, climbed the walls of San Damiano, Clare, ill as she was, had the Blessed Sacrament carried out before them and prayed, and the soldiers fled. That is why she is often shown holding a monstrance. Another story tells that one Christmas, too sick to go to Mass, she saw and heard it on the wall of her room. For that reason Pius XII named her patron of television.

Clare wrote her own Rule, the first rule for women written by a woman. Pope Innocent IV approved it on 9 August 1253, and she died two days later. She was canonized by Alexander IV in 1255. Her sisters, the Poor Clares, still live in enclosed communities around the world.
why_here: The abbey's relic of Clare is a lock of her hair, and that is the very thing Francis cut off on the night she gave her life to God. It is a relic of a young woman's decision, made at eighteen, against her family's plans. The Prep's students are near that age, many of them already thinking about what their lives are for.

Clare is also a saint of stability. She lived over forty years in one small convent, as the monks vow to live in one monastery. She worked with her hands at spinning and sewing, the kind of work the abbey's tailors still do, and she ran her community firmly and kindly for four decades. Her Rule, like Benedict's, puts poverty and prayer at the center.
relic: One relic on the large linen board, labelled "Ex capillis", from her hair.
check: Pius XII's apostolic letter naming her patron of television is dated 1957 and was proclaimed in February 1958; sources give either year.

name: St. Claude de la Colombière
title: Jesuit priest, apostle of the Sacred Heart
summary: St. Claude de la Colombière was a French Jesuit who, as confessor to St. Margaret Mary Alacoque, judged her visions of the Sacred Heart to be from God and spread that devotion. He was imprisoned and banished from England during the panic of the Popish Plot. He has no formal patronage, but he is a good friend to anyone discerning a vocation that does not feel easy at first.
life: Claude de la Colombière was born in 1641 near Lyon, in southeastern France, into a family of the minor nobility. He was taught by the Jesuits and entered their order at seventeen. Later, in his private notes, he admitted that he had felt a strong natural dislike for the life he chose. He was a gifted man, a fine preacher and writer, and taught rhetoric in Jesuit colleges. In 1674, during his long retreat before final vows, he made a private vow to keep the rules of his order perfectly, a vow he held to for the rest of his life.

In 1675 he was sent as superior to the small Jesuit house at Paray-le-Monial in Burgundy. There he became the confessor of a Visitation nun, Margaret Mary Alacoque, who said she had received visions of Christ showing her his heart and asking that it be honored. Her sisters and superiors doubted her. Claude listened carefully, judged that her experience came from God, and encouraged her. He spread the devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus in his own preaching and writing.

In 1676 he was sent to London as preacher to Mary of Modena, the Duchess of York and wife of the future King James II, herself a daughter of the House of Este. At the court of a Protestant country he preached, heard confessions and helped converts back to the Church. In 1678 the panic of the "Popish Plot", a story of a Catholic conspiracy made up by Titus Oates, swept England. Claude was denounced, arrested and held in a damp prison, then banished from England early in 1679.

His lungs never recovered. He returned to France, served as spiritual director to young Jesuits at Lyon, and was sent back to Paray in the hope that the air would help him. He died there on 15 February 1682, at forty-one. His retreat notes and letters were published after his death and are still read, especially his "Act of Confidence in God". He was beatified in 1929 and canonized by John Paul II in 1992.
patronage: devotion to the Sacred Heart (by association, not a formal patronage)
why_here: Claude chose religious life while feeling a strong aversion to it, and he said so honestly. That makes him a good friend for students at the Prep who are discerning their lives, and for young monks in formation, because a vocation does not always feel easy or natural at first. What carried him was trust, which is the theme of his best-known prayer.

He was also a careful listener. He believed a young nun whom others dismissed, after testing what she said. Teachers and monks who hear students' troubles, and priests who hear confessions, can ask for his patient judgment. His prison and exile give him a claim too on the prayers of all who are falsely accused.
relic: One relic on the large linen board, labelled "B. Cl. d. la Colom[bière]", so written between his beatification in 1929 and his canonization in 1992.
check: He has no widely recognized official patronage.

name: Bl. Columba Marmion
title: Abbot of Maredsous, spiritual writer
summary: Bl. Columba Marmion was an Irish priest who became a monk of Maredsous in Belgium and later its third abbot. His conferences to his monks, published as books such as Christ, the Life of the Soul, were read in monasteries and seminaries for decades. He has no official patronage, but he is a natural patron for the abbey's novices and for those who form them.
life: Joseph Marmion was born in Dublin on 1 April 1858, to an Irish father and a French mother. He studied for the priesthood at Clonliffe College in Dublin and at the Irish College in Rome, and was ordained in Rome in 1881. On his way home he visited the Benedictine abbey of Maredsous in Belgium and was drawn to it, but his bishop wanted him in Dublin. For five years he served as a curate and then as a professor of philosophy at Clonliffe, and as chaplain to a convent and a women's prison.

In 1886, with his bishop's leave, he entered Maredsous and took the name Columba, after the Irish monk of Iona. It was hard for him. He was nearly thirty, a priest used to his own ways, now a novice among much younger Belgian men, living in French and under a strict German-trained discipline. He persevered and made his vows in 1888. In 1899 he helped found the abbey of Mont César at Louvain, where he taught theology to young monks and became confessor to Cardinal Mercier, the archbishop of Mechelen.

In 1909 he was elected the third abbot of Maredsous. He was a warm, humorous and approachable abbot, a good preacher, and much in demand for retreats. His conferences to his monks, written down and edited by a fellow monk, became books. Christ, the Life of the Soul (1917), Christ in His Mysteries (1919) and Christ, the Ideal of the Monk (1922) were translated into many languages and read in monasteries, seminaries and convents for decades. Their theme is simple. We become sons of God by grace, in Christ, and the whole spiritual life is to live out that adoption.

When the German army occupied Belgium in 1914, he sent his young monks to Ireland, where they could continue their formation in peace, and he made the difficult wartime journey himself to see to them. The war years were full of worry and debt. He died at Maredsous on 30 January 1923, during an influenza epidemic. John Paul II beatified him in 2000.
patronage: spiritual reading and those who teach the faith (by association)
why_here: Marmion was a Benedictine abbot whose life work was teaching his monks, and the abbey's novice master, abbot and teachers do the same work. His books were long the standard reading in American Benedictine houses and seminaries, and the monks of St. Bernard, who ran a seminary here for years, may well have read him in their formation. He is a modern Benedictine for a modern abbey.

He also entered religious life late and found it hard, and he cared about the formation of young monks enough to move them out of a war zone. His prayers suit the abbey's growing number of novices and juniors, and those who form them. His chief theme, that a Christian is a son or daughter of God in Christ, is a good one for teenagers trying to understand who they are.
relic: A clothing relic, labelled "Ex Indumentis" and "B." (Blessed): in a gilt sunburst (IMG_4891) and in a clear case in the white linen case (IMG_4987), perhaps the same theca photographed twice.
check: Feast 3 October follows the catalogue; some Benedictine calendars may keep 30 January, his death day. He has no official patronage. Whether the abbey's monks used his books in formation is a guess, worded as one; drop it if you prefer.

name: St. Conrad of Parzham
title: Capuchin brother, porter of Altötting
summary: St. Conrad of Parzham was a Bavarian farmer who became a Capuchin lay brother and served for forty-one years as porter of the friary at Altötting, receiving pilgrims, the poor and children with patience. By tradition he is a patron of porters and of Altötting's pilgrims. He suits the abbey's guest masters, and he comes from the same Bavaria as Metten Abbey.
life: Johann Birndorfer was born in 1818 at Parzham, a farming hamlet in Lower Bavaria, one of the many children of a prosperous and devout farm family. He lost both his parents in his teens. He stayed on the farm and worked it for years, praying the rosary as he worked, walking long distances to Mass and to shrines, and joining a lay confraternity. In 1849, at thirty-one, he gave away his share of the inheritance and asked to join the Capuchin friars as a lay brother. He took the name Conrad and made his vows in 1852.

He was sent at once to the friary of St. Anne at Altötting, beside the shrine of the Black Madonna, the most visited place of pilgrimage in Bavaria. He was made porter, the brother who answers the door, and he kept that job for forty-one years. Altötting drew huge crowds, and the friary door was busy all day. Pilgrims came to ask for a priest or for directions, the poor came for food, and children came because he gave them bread and sometimes a holy picture. He answered each with patience, a few words of advice, and often a reminder to pray. People later said that he seldom spoke much but never sent anyone away unheard.

His nights were given to prayer. Near the door there was a small room from which he could see the tabernacle in the church, and he spent much of his spare time there. He fasted and slept little, yet was always calm and cheerful. When he was asked about his life he said that the cross was his book.

In April 1894, old and ill, he gave up his post. He died a few days later, on 21 April. Pilgrims and the people of Altötting at once began to treat him as a saint. He was beatified by Pius XI in 1930 and canonized by the same pope in 1934. His body rests in the friary church, which now bears his name.
why_here: St. Benedict tells the porter of a monastery to answer every knock with "Thanks be to God" and to receive each guest as Christ. Conrad lived exactly that for forty-one years. The abbey's guest masters, the monks who run the Retreat Center, and those who meet pilgrims at the Ave Maria Grotto are doing his work. Abbot Brendan was himself a guest master. Conrad is their natural patron.

He was also a Bavarian farm boy, from the same Catholic Bavaria as Metten Abbey, the mother of St. Vincent and so the grandmother of St. Bernard. Cullman was settled by German immigrants, and some of its families will know Altötting by name. He was beatified in 1930, in the abbey's own lifetime, and the label still calls him Blessed.
relic: One relic in a gilt sunburst (IMG_4977), labelled "B. Konradus à P[arzham]", so written between his beatification in 1930 and his canonization in 1934.
check: His feast, 21 April, is kept in the Capuchin and German calendars, not the General Roman Calendar. The patronage of porters is popular, not formally declared.

name: St. Contardo d'Este
title: Pilgrim, patron of Broni
summary: St. Contardo d'Este, according to the tradition of Broni in Lombardy, was a son of the house of Este who set out as a poor pilgrim to Compostela and died unknown at Broni in 1249. Broni keeps him as its patron, and Modena as a secondary patron. His story of a stranger recognized too late is a lesson for a house that receives guests.
life: Contardo belonged to the house of Este, the noble family that ruled Ferrara and that also gave the Church the two Blessed Beatrices. Almost all that is told of him comes from local tradition at Broni, a small town near Pavia in Lombardy, and from writers who followed it much later, so the story should be read as a tradition, not as a record.

According to that tradition, Contardo turned his back on his family's wealth and set out as a poor pilgrim to the shrine of St. James at Compostela in Spain, one of the three great pilgrimages of the Middle Ages. He travelled on foot, without money or rank, living on what he was given. On the way he fell gravely ill at Broni. Because no one knew who he was, he was turned away or left with nothing better than a poor shed, and he died there unknown, in 1249, at about thirty-three.

The story goes on that after his death signs were seen at the place, a light and a ringing of bells, and that cures were reported. Only then was it learned that the poor stranger was a son of the house of Este. The townspeople buried him with honor in their church of San Pietro, which later became a basilica, and they have kept him as their patron ever since. Pope Paul V approved the local cult in 1609. Modena, which the Este later ruled, also counts him as a secondary patron.
The label in the abbey's reliquary, "S. Contard. Est.", sits on the oval of royal saints and saints of the House of Este, beside the two Beatrices.
why_here: Contardo's story is about a stranger who is not recognized until too late. That is a sobering lesson for a house that receives guests. The monks at the door, at the Retreat Center and at the Grotto meet pilgrims every day, and they cannot know who any of them is. St. Benedict's answer, to receive every guest as Christ, is what Broni learned too late.

He is also a patron for the journey itself. Many Prep students travel long distances to the school, some from abroad. Pilgrims to the Grotto come from all over, and the abbey's Retreat Center welcomes others on their way. Contardo, who set out poor and did not arrive, is a friend to all who are on the road and to those who fall ill there.
relic: One relic on the oval of royal saints and saints of the House of Este (IMG_4912–4915), labelled "S. Contard. Est."
check: Feast 16 April and the approval of his cult by Paul V in 1609 come from secondary sources; his exact place in the Este family is disputed, so it is left out. Some sources call him Blessed rather than Saint; the abbey's label says "S.".

name: St. Dominic
title: Founder of the Order of Preachers
summary: St. Dominic was a Castilian canon who preached on foot and in poverty in southern France and founded the Order of Preachers, sending his friars to study and preach in the universities and towns. He is a patron of astronomers and of the falsely accused. He is the name saint of Fr. Dominic, the abbey's subprior and a math teacher at the Prep.
life: Domingo de Guzmán was born about 1170 at Caleruega, in Old Castile in Spain. The name on his label, "de Guzmán", is his family name. He studied arts and theology at Palencia for some ten years. His first biographer, Jordan of Saxony, tells that during a famine there he sold his books, precious handwritten copies with his own notes, to feed the poor, saying he would not study on dead skins while living men starved. He became a canon of the cathedral of Osma, living a common life of prayer under the Rule of St. Augustine.

In 1203 and 1205 he travelled north with his bishop, Diego of Osma, on missions for the king of Castile, and passed through Languedoc in southern France. The Albigensian or Cathar heresy had spread there, teaching that the material world was evil. The papal legates sent to answer it came with horses, servants and fine clothes, and won no one. Diego and Dominic told them to preach as the apostles had, on foot and begging their bread. Dominic stayed in the region for about ten years, preaching, debating in public, and in 1206 founded a house at Prouille for women who had left the Cathars. The crusade against the Albigensians, which began in 1209, was a war fought by others, and the later Inquisition was not his work.

In 1215 he gathered a small band of preachers at Toulouse, and in 1216 Pope Honorius III approved them as the Order of Preachers. Dominic did a bold thing. In 1217 he scattered his few friars, sending them to Paris, Bologna, Madrid and Rome, to the universities and the growing towns, to study and preach. He insisted on study as a duty, gave his order a system of elected superiors, and wanted the friars to live poor. He spent the last years of his life on the road. He died at Bologna on 6 August 1221 and was canonized in 1234.

The rosary is linked with his name by long tradition, including a story that Our Lady gave it to him. That is a pious tradition, not a settled historical fact. The prayer grew over centuries, and Dominican friars did much to spread it later on. His friars still keep his motto, to contemplate and to hand on to others the fruits of contemplation.
why_here: Dominic is the name saint of Fr. Dominic, the abbey's subprior and a math teacher at the Prep. A Castilian canon who sent his friars to the universities and made study a part of holiness is a fitting patron for a monk who teaches. Dominic did not think learning and prayer were at odds, and neither does a Benedictine school.

For the students, he is the young man who sold his books to feed the hungry. Study mattered to him, but people mattered more. He also learned that argument wins no one when it comes with pride and comfort, and that the truth is best offered with humility. That is worth knowing for Scholars' Bowl players and debaters, and for anyone who wants to share the faith. Abbey and school keep three relics of him.
relic: Three relics: a gilt sunburst labelled "S. Dominici de Guzm[an]" (IMG_4890), a theca on the large linen board labelled "S. Dominici C." (of St. Dominic, Confessor), and one label on the oval of fifteen relics (4965).
check: His patronage of astronomers is traditional, from the legend of a star on his forehead.

name: St. Dymphna
title: Virgin and martyr of Geel
summary: St. Dymphna is known only from a 13th-century legend of an Irish princess who fled her father and was killed by him at Geel, in what is now Belgium. What is history is Geel's care for people with mental illness, which grew into a system of family care that still exists. She is patron of those with mental illness, and her prayers can be asked for students who struggle.
life: Dymphna is known to us from a Latin life written in the 13th century, at the request of the bishop of Cambrai, by a canon named Peter. He said he drew on old oral tradition. No earlier record of her survives, so her story is a legend, possibly built on an older cult around two tombs found at Geel, in what is now Belgium. It should be read as a legend.

In the story, Dymphna was the daughter of a pagan king in Ireland and a Christian mother, who had her secretly baptized. When her mother died, the king was wild with grief and wanted to marry a woman just like her. His advisers told him there was none like her except his own daughter. Dymphna, then fourteen, fled across the sea with her confessor, an old priest named Gerebernus, and a few companions, and they settled near Geel. Her father tracked them down. His men killed the priest, and when Dymphna still refused him, the king struck off her head with his own sword.

What is history is Geel itself. A church was built over the relics, and from the Middle Ages people with mental illness were brought there in hope of healing. Records show a sick house beside the church by the 14th century. Pilgrims who stayed for a novena needed lodging, and the townspeople began taking them into their homes. Over the centuries this became a custom and then a system of family care that still exists, in which people with mental illness live as boarders with families in the town, helped by a public psychiatric service. It is often cited as one of the oldest forms of community care in the world.

For that reason Dymphna is the patron of those who suffer from mental illness and of those who care for them. Her feast is kept in Geel and in many places, though she is not in the General Roman Calendar.
patronage: those with mental illness and nervous disorders
victims of abuse within the family
why_here: Depression and anxiety are real among teenagers, and a boarding school, where students live far from home, has to take them seriously. Dymphna is a fourteen-year-old who fled home to escape harm. Her legend is grim, but what grew from it at Geel is good. A whole town took troubled people into its homes and treated them as family. That is exactly the kind of help her intercession points to, prayer alongside real care, never prayer instead of it.

Her prayers can be asked for students and their families, for teachers and dorm staff who notice when someone is struggling, and for anyone in the abbey or the school who carries a hidden burden of mind.
relic: One relic on a modern pewter plaque, in the case lined in white linen (IMG_4980).
